output.title: Why reviewer training is not enough
output.body:
Reviewer training helps, but it is not a complete control. If the same approval rules are applied every time, the real risk is often not knowledge. It is repeatable logic, data entry slips, fatigue, or edge cases that training alone will not remove. That is the practical limit: training can improve judgment, but it does not change the workflow itself.

The question I would ask is simple: are most errors happening because the reviewer does not know the rule, or because the rule is repeated and the work still needs manual checking? If it is the second case, you are looking at a workflow problem, not a classroom problem.

A plain example: if invoice or approval checks always follow the same sequence, a tired person can still miss one step. A rule check can catch that kind of miss; a slide deck cannot. That is not a complaint about people. It is just how late afternoons work.

At Bareni, we focus on repeatable logic steps in small-business workflows, with human approval kept in place for exceptions and high-risk decisions. That is policy, not a guarantee.

So the next step is to identify one recurring decision step that follows the same logic each time and note how often it appears. If it is truly repeatable, it is worth separating from reviewer training before you spend more time on materials.
